• Common name: Duckweed
  • Difficulty: easy
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Water hardness: soft to hard (does not matter)
  • Substrate: not needed
  • Growth rate: very fast
  • Placement in tank: floating
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed
  • Propagation: division
  • Colour: light green to dark green

Duckweeds are very small, free-floating aquatic plants, also known as Bayroot, Water lentils or Water lenses. There are 5 known genera: Spirodela, Landoltia, Lemna, Wolffiella and Wolffia. More than 40 species exist, 9 of them occurring in North America. Common Duckweed (Lemna minor) is the most widespread species and has a subcosmopolitan distribution, ranging across Canada and the United States, Southeast Asia and Europe.

Duckweed grows in freshwater ponds and slow-moving streams on virtually all continents except Antarctica, from tropical to temperate regions. It spreads rapidly across quiet, nutrient-rich water and grows best where annual daytime temperatures range between 15 and 32 °C.

When the water body dries out or temperatures decline, Duckweed persists until conditions that support growth return. This happens through late-summer flowering or the production of starch-filled turions, which are denser than the fronds, so the plants sink to the bottom and become embedded in dried mud.

The plants have a simple oval structure and lack an obvious stem or leaves. Most of each plant is a small "thallus" or "frond", 1–8 mm long and 0.6–5 mm broad. Fronds attach to one another and form an extensive mat on the water surface. The roots of Spirodela and Lemna are adventitious, from a few millimetres up to 15 cm long, and help stabilise the plant and absorb nutrients.

Duckweed is easy to grow and needs no special care. To plant it, simply place it on the water surface and dose nutrients to aid acclimatisation. It is perennial and lives more than 2 years under optimal conditions.

It grows fast, so monitor it and scoop out a reasonable quantity when it covers the whole water surface. Provide moderate to high light (preferably high), very slow water currents and a regular supply of nutrients.

If a hang-on-back filter with strong flow pushes Duckweed around the tank, growth slows. Redirect the flow 10–12 cm below the water surface, which also avoids plant particles clogging the filter. Another solution is to create a roped-off area using clear air tubing strung across the top of the aquarium, or to place extra sponge pieces where water exits to slow the flow.

Propagation: in aquariums Duckweed mainly reproduces by cloning. When mature, it creates new buds in the centre of the frond, which turn into new fronds while still attached to the parent. Once fully mature they separate and start producing their own copies. The plant needs only 16 hours to double its biomass, so it can cover an aquarium in next to no time. Flowering is rare (it has the smallest flower in the world, visible only with a magnifying glass).

Problems:

  • Fast growth: explosive growth once nutrient levels are high; it can cover the entire surface and be difficult to control.
  • Light penetration: dense mats may block light from reaching submerged plants.
  • Oxygen depletion: without aeration or surface movement, a thick layer left for long can deplete oxygen and suffocate fish or shrimp.
  • Yellowing: can indicate nutrient deficiency or lack of light.
  • Hard to remove: once settled it is extremely hard to get rid of (unless you have plant-eating fish such as goldfish), and it sticks like glue to any surface.

Removal: turn off filters and aeration, scoop it from the surface, check every surface including the glass rim, the filter and other plants (it can survive underwater for a long time), and repeat the next day. Do not share equipment between tanks. If the setup allows, reducing light and increasing water flow also helps control it.

Quarantine: unless the plant was grown in sterile in-vitro conditions in an undamaged pot, quarantine and disinfect it first with bleach or potassium permanganate. It can carry parasites, snails or predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs), or be treated with pesticides that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Water temperature: Duckweed grows optimally between 15 and 32 °C. Above or below that range it just sits there and does not grow.

pH: it survives at pH 5.0–9.0 but grows best at 6.5–7.5.

Hardness: in general Duckweed does not care about hardness and tolerates soft or hard water. For optimal growth, keep 2–15 GH and 1–12 KH. Some species, such as Lemna minor, can even tolerate low salinity (0.5–2.5 percent sodium chloride), while others prefer freshwater.

Water flow: Duckweed inhabits ponds and shallow streams with slow current and often does not survive in fast-moving water (above 0.3 m/s). Still or slow water is recommended.

Tank size: Duckweed can be grown anywhere, including a 4-litre tank. It is a good choice for nano aquariums.

Lighting: in nature it grows in open ponds with little shade, and direct sunlight suits it best. That is not suitable for aquariums with other plants and animals that may not appreciate direct sunlight or very powerful artificial light. Full-spectrum LED lighting will suffice; provide medium to high lighting so the plant can photosynthesise and grow better. Incandescent bulbs are not recommended, as they give off a great deal of heat which can overheat the plant and the tank water.

Substrate: Duckweed is a floating plant, so it has no specific substrate requirements.

CO2 and fertiliser: it does not require CO2 dosing, as it gets it from the air. To increase growth, provide fertilisers (NPK – nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium) or supplements regularly.

If you keep shrimp with Duckweed, note that copper (found in most fertilisers) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Duckweed is quite high in protein: studies give an average of 37.0% crude protein. It can be used as a food source for fish, shrimp, snails, crayfish and crabs. To make a food, blend it with montmorillonite clay as a binder, spread it thinly, let it dry completely, then break it into small pieces and feed.

Benefits:

  • Aesthetics: lush green cover that mimics a pond.
  • Filtration: absorbs phosphates, nitrates, ammonia and toxins; probably the most efficient nitrate-absorbing plant.
  • Algae control: shades out algae and reduces its growth.
  • Shelter: fish, fry and shrimp use it as cover and appreciate the shade.
  • Light filtering: useful for plants that need little light (Java fern, Amazon sword, Marimo moss ball, Anubias).
  • Prevents fish from jumping when there is no lid.
  • Indicator: very bright green often means it is absorbing a lot of nutrients, which may signal water quality problems; darker colour usually means the water is cleaner. Roots elongate quickly when nutrient levels drop.

Tankmates: easy to keep with fish (guppies, mollies, swordtails, loaches, discus, platies, tetras, zebra danios, otocinclus), shrimp of any species and snails. Herbivorous fish such as plecos, goldfish, cichlids, rosy barbs, silver dollars and tilapia, and some snails, are likely to eat it. Most carnivorous fish will not touch it. It suits crab and crayfish tanks.

Buying: available in pet stores and online. Handle with care, and check that roots and fronds are in good condition without discolouration or brown or yellow spots.

Interesting facts:

  • Used in genetic and biomedical research.
  • Acts as a bioremediator, removing heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, cadmium, copper and zinc from water.
  • Studied as a possible source of clean, renewable energy.
  • A cover of Duckweed significantly reduces water evaporation.
  • Contains more protein than soybeans and is a potential food source in parts of Southeast Asia; also used as fodder for ducks and in broiler diets.
  • Can be carried between regions by migrating birds, wind or water current.
